# Introduction
> _Estimate the difference in weight change between quitters and non-quitters, and its uncertainty, in situations where the standard formulas either don’t exist or might not be appropriate._

This report uses bootstrapping to estimate the uncertainty associated with differences in median weight change between participants who quit smoking and those who continued smoking. The standard error of a median is difficult to calculate and bootstrapping provides a robust alternative.



The methods section describes how bootstrapping is used for this analysis. The results section presents the findings, and the discussion section interprets the results and discusses limitations.

# Methods
> _What you did and why, including the key decisions you made and the assumptions of the method. Someone else should be able to repeat your analysis from this section._


The analysis uses data from the the first US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey Epidemiologic Follow-up Study (NHEFS). This study followed 1629 participants between 1971 and 1982 and observed weight change in smokers. The exposure used in this analysis is smoking status (quitters versus non-quitters). 

The analysis method can be divided into four phases: data preparation and descriptive statistics, bootstrapping the difference in median, regression analysis to estimate the adjusted effect of smoking cessation and last and last, monte carlo method to determine error.

**Data preparation and descriptive statistics:** Cases with missing values in the weight change (`wt82_71`) variable were excluded from the analysis. In total 62 entries were removed, leaving `r n_total` participants for analysis. 

**Bootstrapping the difference in medians:** 5000 bootstrap samples were drawn with replacement from the original dataset, using the stratified bootstrap method. For each sample, the median weight change was calculated for both quitters and non-quitters, and the difference in medians was computed. The distribution of these differences across all bootstrap samples was used to estimate the standard error and construct confidence intervals.

**Regression to determine the adjusted effect of quitting:** Ordinary least squares regression was used to estimate the adjusted effect of quitting smoking on weight change, controlling for baseline weight and other covariates. The regression model was fitted to each bootstrap sample to obtain a distribution of the adjusted effect estimates.

**Monte Carlo error:** Last, a Monte Carlo simulation was run to determine the variability in the bootstrap estimates due to the finite number of bootstrap samples. This was done by repeating the bootstrapping procedure 20 times and examining the variability in the resulting estimates.

Next, the results of the analysis are presented.

> Note: NB - Remember to consider sample in groups


# Results
> A small number of well-chosen tables and figures, with estimates and measures of uncertainty.


In total, data for 1929 participants were recorded. Missing values in the weight change (`wt82_71`) variable were excluded from the analysis (`r pct_missing`%), leaving `r n_total` participants for analysis. 27 of `r n_missing` missing values were from participants who died, biasing the analysis to healthier and younger individuals.

__Descriptive statistics:__
Of the `r n_total` participants, `r n_quit` (`r round(100 * n_quit / n_total, 1)`%) quit smoking while `r n_cont` participants continued smoking until 1982. The median weight change was `r round(med_diff, 2)` kg higher among those who quit smoking (`r round(med_quit, 2)` kg) than those who continued smoking (`r round(med_cont, 2)` kg).

__Bootstrapping the difference in medians:__
Bootsrapping the difference in median weight change between quitters and non-quitters produced a mean estimate of `r round(median_boot$t0, 2)` kg with a standard error of `r round(median_se, 2)` kg. The 95% confidence interval for the difference in medians was estimated to be `r sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", median_ci$percent[4], median_ci$percent[5])` kg using the percentile method and `r sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", median_ci$bca[4], median_ci$bca[5])` kg using the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) method (@tbl-median-boot).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-median-boot
#| tbl-cap: 'Bootstrap estimates for the difference in median weight change`#linebreak()`{=typst}`#text(size: 0.85em, style: "italic")[R = 5000, stratified by smoking status]`{=typst}'
#| echo: false

library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

median_table <- data.frame(
  Method   = c("Percentile", "BCa"),
  Estimate = rep(median_boot$t0, 2),
  Bias     = rep(mean(median_boot$t[, 1]) - median_boot$t0, 2),
  SE       = rep(median_se, 2),
  CI_Lower = c(median_ci$percent[4], median_ci$bca[4]),
  CI_Upper = c(median_ci$percent[5], median_ci$bca[5])
)

median_table$CI <- sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", median_table$CI_Lower, median_table$CI_Upper)

tab <- kable(median_table[, c("Method", "Estimate", "Bias", "SE", "CI")],
             digits = 3, align = "lcccc", booktabs = TRUE,
             col.names = c("CI method", "Estimate (kg)", "Bias", "SE", "95% CI"))

if (knitr::is_html_output() || knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  tab <- tab |>
    kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, latex_options = "HOLD_position") |>
    row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#053259")
}

tab
```


__Regression to determine the adjusted effect of quitting:__

Conventional OLS assumes the residuals has homoscedasticity, are independent and normally distributed. 

Case bootstrap resamples whole participants with replacement, treating the predictors as random. It refits the model 5000 times and use the spread of the coefficients to determine the standard error, resulting in a slighlty wider confidence interval. An advantage is that it can be employed under heteroscedasticity and it does not assume constant variance. 

Residual bootstrap treats the covariates as fixed, keeping the predictors as the observed values. It uses the fitted values from the model and resamples from the residuals. The confidence interval is slightly narrower than the case bootstrap, but it assumes that the model is correctly specified and that the residuals are independent and identically distributed.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression-boot
#| tbl-cap: 'Adjusted effect of quitting smoking on weight change`#linebreak()`{=typst}`#text(size: 0.85em, style: "italic")[Conventional vs bootstrap standard errors; R = 5000, percentile 95% CIs for bootstrap methods]`{=typst}'
#| echo: false

comparison_tab <- data.frame(
  Method   = comparison$Method,
  Estimate = sprintf("%.2f", comparison$Estimate),
  SE       = sprintf("%.3f", comparison$SE),
  CI       = sprintf("(%.2f, %.2f)", comparison$CI_Lower, comparison$CI_Upper)
)

knitr::kable(comparison_tab, align = "lccc", row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Method", "Estimate (kg)", "SE", "95% CI"))
```


```{r}
#| label: fig-resid
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the adjusted regression model."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Residuals versus fitted values"
#|   - "Residuals by smoking status"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| echo: false

par(col.main = uct_cols["navy"], col.lab = uct_cols["navy"],
    col.axis = uct_cols["navy"], fg = uct_cols["navy"])

plot(fitted(model), resid(model),
     pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = adjustcolor(uct_cols["blue"], alpha.f = 0.5),
     xlab = "Fitted weight change (kg)", ylab = "Residual (kg)", main = "")
abline(h = 0, col = uct_cols["magenta"], lty = 2, lwd = 2)

par(col.main = uct_cols["navy"], col.lab = uct_cols["navy"],
    col.axis = uct_cols["navy"], fg = uct_cols["navy"])

boxplot(resid(model) ~ dat$qsmk,
        names = c("Non-quitters", "Quitters"),
        col = uct_cols[c("blue", "teal")], border = uct_cols["navy"],
        xlab = "", ylab = "Residual (kg)", main = "")
```

# Appendix A: Missing data {.unnumbered}

Weight change (`wt82_71`) was missing for `r n_missing` of `r nrow(nhefs)` participants (`r sprintf("%.1f", pct_missing)`%). @tbl-missingness compares their baseline characteristics with those of participants who had an observed outcome.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missingness
#| tbl-cap: 'Baseline characteristics of participants with missing and observed weight change`#linebreak()`{=typst}`#text(size: 0.85em, style: "italic")[SMD = standardised mean difference; p-values from Welch t-tests]`{=typst}'
#| echo: false

miss_labels <- c(
  age            = "Age (years)",
  wt71           = "Weight in 1971 (kg)",
  ht             = "Height (cm)",
  smokeintensity = "Cigarettes per day",
  smokeyrs       = "Years smoked",
  income         = "Income category",
  cholesterol    = "Cholesterol (mg/dL)",
  sbp            = "Systolic BP (mmHg)",
  dbp            = "Diastolic BP (mmHg)"
)

miss_cont_tab <- data.frame(
  Variable = miss_labels[miss_cont$Variable],
  Missing  = sprintf("%.1f", miss_cont$Mean_Missing),
  Observed = sprintf("%.1f", miss_cont$Mean_Observed),
  SMD      = sprintf("%.2f", miss_cont$SMD),
  p        = ifelse(miss_cont$p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", miss_cont$p))
)

knitr::kable(
  miss_cont_tab, align = "lcccc", row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Variable",
                sprintf("Missing (n = %d)", n_missing),
                sprintf("Observed (n = %d)", nrow(nhefs) - n_missing),
                "SMD", "p")
)
```
